## Introduction

Febrile seizures are generalized seizures that typically occur in children between 6 months and 5 years of age, in association with a fever greater than 100.4 °F (38 °C), in the absence of a central nervous system (CNS) infection, a known seizure-provoking etiology (eg, electrolyte imbalance, hypoglycemia, or substance exposure), or a history of afebrile seizure. No specific fever threshold is required to trigger a febrile seizure, as the convulsive temperature threshold varies from patient to patient. Recognized risk factors include underlying neurologic impairment, concurrent viral infection, a family history of seizures, developmental delay, low serum zinc and iron levels, and maternal smoking or stress during pregnancy.

Most febrile seizures are self-limited and resolve without complications, although some evidence suggests a subset of patients carries a higher subsequent risk of epilepsy or another seizure disorder; proposed explanations include an underlying neurologic predisposition or an effect of the seizure itself on a still-developing nervous system. Febrile seizures are classified as simple, involving a single seizure lasting 15 minutes or less, or complex, involving multiple seizures within 24 hours, focal features, or a duration of 15 minutes or more. Simple febrile seizures account for the majority of cases. Febrile status epilepticus, defined as a seizure lasting longer than 30 minutes, is an uncommon subset associated with worse outcomes than simple febrile seizures.

Evaluation centers on characterizing the seizure type and identifying the underlying cause of fever through focused history, examination, and, when indicated, diagnostic testing. Most febrile seizures resolve spontaneously and can be managed expectantly; complex or prolonged seizures may instead require pharmacologic therapy to terminate seizure activity. This activity is designed to strengthen clinicians' competence in managing febrile seizures, equipping the interprofessional team with current knowledge and strategies for evaluation, timely treatment, and coordinated care that improves patient outcomes.

## Etiology

Febrile seizures are generalized seizures, typically occurring in children between 6 months and 5 years of age, in association with a fever greater than 100.4 °F (38 °C), in the absence of a CNS infection, a known seizure-provoking etiology (eg, electrolyte imbalance, hypoglycemia, or substance exposure), or a history of afebrile seizure. No specific fever threshold is required to trigger a febrile seizure, as the convulsive temperature threshold varies from patient to patient. Recognized risk factors include underlying neurologic impairment, concurrent viral infection, a family history of seizures, developmental delay, low serum zinc and iron levels, and maternal smoking or stress during pregnancy.

An estimated 10% to 33% of patients have a first-degree relative with a positive seizure history, with concordance rates of approximately 35% to 69% in monozygotic twins and 14% to 20% in dizygotic twins, suggesting a genetic contribution to febrile seizure susceptibility. Inheritance appears to follow an autosomal dominant pattern with reduced penetrance in some families and a polygenic or multifactorial pattern in others, with candidate loci identified on chromosomes 1q31, 2q23-34, 3p24.2-23, 3q26.2-26.33, 5q14-15, 5q34, 6q22-24, 8q13-21, 18p11-2, 19p13-3, 19q, and 21q22.

The risk of febrile seizure may relate more to the peak temperature reached during a fever than to the rate of temperature rise. Seizure threshold itself varies by individual and changes with age and development; infants carry a higher baseline risk, and premature infants, particularly those who received postnatal corticosteroids, are at even greater risk. Infants also tend to have a lower seizure threshold overall, which certain medications and electrolyte disturbances (eg, hyponatremia) can further reduce. Deficiencies in iron, zinc, vitamin B12, folic acid, selenium, calcium, and magnesium have each been associated with an increased risk of febrile seizures. A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 case-control studies comprising 3,856 children found that hemoglobin, mean corpuscular volume, serum iron, and ferritin were each significantly lower in children with febrile seizures than in febrile children without seizures, supporting iron status as a modifiable, screenable risk factor in children with recurrent events.

No single etiology of fever predominates, though viral infections are more commonly implicated than bacterial infections. Roseolovirus is the most common virus associated with febrile seizures in the United States and European countries; primary infection affects most children by 2 years of age, and is estimated to account for up to one-third of first febrile seizures in this age group.[Gagadam, S et al. Systematic review of HHV-6 and febrile seizures: Should the ER include it in the viral panel?. 2025] Other studies have found that febrile seizures secondary to Roseolovirus are associated with a higher incidence of complex features, recurrence, and febrile status epilepticus.

A 2025 systematic review of HHV-6 in pediatric febrile seizures reached a similar conclusion, finding that primary HHV-6B infection is disproportionately associated with complex febrile seizures and febrile status epilepticus; the authors noted that selective testing may be reasonable in children with prolonged or recurrent events, but that routine emergency department viral panel testing for HHV-6 is not yet supported by strong enough evidence to be recommended broadly.[Gagadam, S et al. Systematic review of HHV-6 and febrile seizures: Should the ER include it in the viral panel?. 2025] In Asian countries, however, influenza A has been frequently associated with febrile seizures. Other commonly associated viral infections include human *herpesvirus 7 (*HHV-7), human coronavirus HKU1, adenovirus, RSV, cytomegalovirus, Shigella, and herpes simplex virus (HSV).

Vaccines have also been shown to transiently increase the risk of febrile seizures in the days following inoculation, including with DTaP-IPV-Hib, MMRV, conjugated pneumococcal vaccine, and some inactivated influenza vaccine formulations. This risk, while low, rises slightly when multiple vaccines are given concurrently; one study estimated a maximum absolute excess risk of 30 febrile seizures per 100,000 vaccinated persons with concomitant administration of IIV3, PCV, and DTaP-containing vaccines, compared with administration on separate days.

## Pathophysiology

The precise pathophysiology of febrile seizures remains incompletely understood, but current evidence points to an interplay of genetic predisposition, age-related immaturity and vulnerability of the central nervous system, and environmental factors. In this framework, the immature brain, subject to fever-enhanced neuronal excitability, is more susceptible to seizure activity, explaining why febrile seizures occur predominantly in children younger than 3 years.

## History and Physical

Clinical History

A comprehensive medical history and a detailed description of the seizure event are essential to evaluating a possible febrile seizure. Because febrile seizures most commonly affect young children, a parent or caregiver is often the primary source of history, including vaccination and immunization status, family history of seizures, recent illness, developmental history, toxin exposure, and personal medical history. Clinicians should also obtain the interval from fever onset to seizure onset, along with the seizure's appearance, duration, and any postictal symptoms, as these details help distinguish simple from complex febrile seizures.

Simple febrile seizures typically present as a single episode of generalized tonic-clonic activity, often involving the face and respiratory muscles, lasting less than 15 minutes and followed by brief postictal drowsiness. Complex febrile seizures, by contrast, involve focal features (usually limited to 1 side of the body), last 15 minutes or longer, or recur within 24 hours, and are frequently followed by postictal weakness or paralysis on the affected side (ie, Todd paralysis). Both types may be accompanied by loss of consciousness, foaming at the mouth, shortness of breath, or cyanosis. Clinicians should also assess for signs of CNS infection or underlying structural abnormalities to distinguish a true febrile seizure from a more serious illness presenting with seizure.

Physical Examination

After the seizure resolves, a general physical and neurologic examination should confirm the child's return to neurologic baseline; persistent acute neurologic impairment (eg, headache, cognitive dysfunction, or weakness) should prompt consideration of alternative diagnoses. Serial vital signs should be obtained, and the exam should look for clues to the underlying cause of fever, eg, erythematous or bulging tympanic membranes, pharyngeal erythema, tonsillar enlargement or inflammation, nuchal rigidity, a bulging or tense fontanelle, or a positive Brudzinski sign. A complete neurologic examination, including fundoscopy to assess for increased intracranial pressure, is warranted. Dermatologic findings may also point to an underlying etiology, including a unilateral port-wine stain (Sturge-Weber syndrome), hypopigmented macules (tuberous sclerosis), or cafe au lait spots and Lisch nodules (neurofibromatosis). See "Tuberous Sclerosis Complex" and "Lisch Nodules" for further information.
